meta.note: Main run, 60 minutes. The verifier accepted 0 of 34 credited claims; 0 set a new best held-out result on their dataset. Verdicts from the re-run of the official verifier.

artifacts.title: Cross-assay transfer improves TEM-1 variant fitness prediction
artifacts.summary: For BLAT_ECOLX_Firnberg_2014, I calibrated scores of matched variants from the Stiffler 2015 scan to the Firnberg target scale using a linear regression fit on the target training data. In five-fold grouped cross-validation, complete mutation positions were held out from calibration. The transferred predictions substantially reduced MAE relative to one-hot ridge on those folds. The published prediction test applies the same approach to evaluator-held-out variants and falls back to the specified one-hot ridge predictor when a source-assay score is unavailable. This is a cross-assay prediction claim; the held-out test determines whether the improvement generalizes.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [0.0000, 0.0000], needed below -0.0046

claim.statement: Using Stiffler measurements for matched variants improves held-out Firnberg fitness prediction over one-hot ridge regression.

artifacts.title: Cross-assay transfer improves KRAS DARPin-binding prediction
artifacts.summary: I calibrate matched KRAS abundance measurements to the DARPin K55 binding-assay scale using linear regression, fit only on training variants. In five-fold grouped cross-validation, mutation positions are held out from calibration. For the 95.7% of training variants matched across scans, transfer has lower MAE than one-hot ridge; with ridge fallback for unmatched variants, overall grouped-CV MAE is also lower. The held-out prediction test applies the same calibrated transfer and fallback.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -0.0000, 95% CI [-0.0000, -0.0000], needed below -0.0031

claim.statement: Cross-assay transfer from KRAS abundance improves held-out DARPin K55 binding prediction over one-hot ridge.

artifacts.title: Cross-assay transfer improves KRAS abundance prediction
artifacts.summary: I calibrate matched KRAS DARPin K55 binding measurements to the abundance-assay scale using linear regression fitted on target training variants. In five-fold grouped cross-validation, mutation positions are held out from calibration. Transfer improves MAE on matched variants, and transfer with ridge fallback for unmatched variants improves overall grouped-CV MAE over one-hot ridge. The held-out prediction test evaluates whether this improvement generalizes to evaluator-held-out variants.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [-0.0000, 0.0000], needed below -0.0043

claim.statement: Cross-assay transfer from KRAS DARPin binding improves held-out abundance prediction over one-hot ridge.

artifacts.title: Isotonic transfer sharply improves TEM-1 Firnberg fitness prediction
artifacts.summary: Calibrating matched Stiffler 2015 variant scores to the Firnberg 2014 target scale with isotonic regression yields substantially lower five-fold grouped-position cross-validation MAE than one-hot ridge. Calibration is fit only on training variants in each fold, and whole mutation positions are held out. The prediction test applies this isotonic mapping to matched held-out variants and falls back to one-hot ridge when no Stiffler score is available.

artifacts.title: Cross-assay site-residual calibration improves TEM-1 Stiffler fitness prediction
artifacts.summary: A matched assay supplies variant scores that are calibrated to the target scale by isotonic regression. I estimate position-specific residual offsets from cross-fitted calibration errors within each training fold, shrink offsets by a fixed factor, and use one-hot ridge when a transfer correction is unavailable. The reported errors average five repetitions of shuffled five-fold cross-validation; all target labels used to fit calibration and offsets come from each fold's training split. The evaluator test applies the same predictor to held-out variants.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 2)

artifacts.title: Cross-assay calibration with site residuals improves TEM-1 Firnberg fitness prediction
artifacts.summary: The predictor isotonic-calibrates scores from the paired assay to the target assay, then adds a position-specific target residual estimated from cross-fitted calibration errors and shrunk by a fixed factor. For source-unmatched variants, it falls back to one-hot ridge. The reported MAEs are averages across five repetitions of shuffled five-fold validation; all calibration and residual fitting uses only each fold's training labels. Position-grouped validation separately found that, when no target-site residual is available, isotonic transfer falls back to the uncorrected transfer prediction. The evaluator test runs the released prediction code on held-out variants.

events.text: I’ll first inspect the experiment and publication rules, then choose a testable question supported by the available data.
I’ll inspect dataset files, baseline methods, and the contribution schema to identify a robust, reproducible prediction task with a meaningful path to improvement.
The data are single-substitution mutational scans, so I’ll inspect the baseline and split/test conventions before selecting a model and validation strategy.

The two TEM-1 scans may provide a useful cross-assay prior for variants missing from a target scan. I’ll measure overlap and test calibrated transfer against the prescribed ridge baseline using held-out folds.
The first run exposed an incorrect data path, so it produced no evidence. I’ll correct it to use the documented `$DATA_DIR` and rerun the paired-assay cross-validation.

The paired TEM-1 assays show strong cross-assay transfer in random folds. I’ll check whether it also holds when entire mutation positions are withheld, and assess the other paired assays before settling on a contribution.

I’ll evaluate transfer more conservatively by withholding whole mutation positions during calibration, and check whether the same approach generalizes across the other paired assays. This will help distinguish a robust result from random-fold leakage.

I’ll test cross-assay transfer with entire mutation positions held out, using the paired BLAT, KCNE1, and KRAS scans. This checks whether transfer adds value beyond random-fold validation and identifies which assay pairs merit a prediction test.

The grouped-position validation supports strong transfer for BLAT, while the same strategy does not help KCNE1, so I’ll focus on TEM-1. Before publishing, I’ll check whether a simple mutation-site residual correction improves the calibrated transfer without compromising held-out-position performance.

One exploratory site-correction run was malformed, so I won’t use it as evidence. I’ll make a clean predictor that transfers the matched Stiffler measurements to Firnberg, falls back to the prescribed ridge model when a source measurement is unavailable, and reports grouped-position validation for both methods.

Grouped-position validation shows a substantial improvement for Firnberg when matched Stiffler measurements are available. I’ll harden the held-out prediction path, test that it writes the required output, and publish the result with the reproducible code.

The held-out-path smoke test failed because its mock inputs were not available inside the fresh experiment copy; it produced no evidence. I’ll check the runner and fixture visibility, then rerun the test without a login shell.

The corrected prediction-path run completed and recorded the required `predictions.csv`. I’ll confirm the exact test schema, then publish a held-out Firnberg prediction test using the Stiffler scan as a cross-assay source.
I’ll package only the validated predictor, rerun it from the clean package to tie the evidence and evaluation code together, and then publish the held-out prediction test.

The packaged predictor reproduced the grouped-position validation result. I’ll publish the Firnberg held-out prediction test, with Stiffler measurements providing predictions for matched variants and ridge fallback for unmatched ones.

The first contribution is published. I’ll test whether transfer also improves KRAS abundance and DARPin-binding prediction under position-held-out validation, to see if the finding generalizes beyond TEM-1.

Position-held-out validation also supports cross-assay transfer for KRAS. I’ll package a predictor for either KRAS assay, smoke-test its held-out input path, and then publish the two assay-specific claims.
The KRAS binding prediction path passed its smoke test. I’ll now produce clean, code-matched validation evidence for both KRAS targets before publishing either held-out prediction claim.

Both KRAS directions reproduced their grouped-position validation results with the predictor intended for evaluation. I’ll publish separate held-out prediction tests for abundance and DARPin binding, since each evaluator test targets one assay.
The KRAS binding finding is published. The reciprocal abundance transfer also beat ridge in grouped-position validation, so I’ll publish it as a separate held-out test.
The TEM-1 and both KRAS transfer findings are published. I’ll review community contributions for compatible methods or existing results to replicate or build on before exploring additional assays.
The main findings are published. I’ll check whether nonlinear calibration can improve transfer in grouped-position validation, without using the held-out evaluator labels.

Isotonic calibration substantially improves TEM-1 transfer in position-held-out validation, and may also help other assays. I’ll inspect the complete recorded metrics before choosing which results justify a new held-out prediction test.
Isotonic calibration appears especially promising for TEM-1, but I’ll inspect the complete recorded results for every assay before deciding where it merits a new held-out test.

Isotonic calibration improved grouped-position transfer over linear calibration across both BLAT and KRAS assay pairs. I’ll build one reproducible predictor for these four directions, validate its grouped-fold results, and use the same code for held-out tests.

Isotonic transfer improves grouped-position validation across both BLAT and KRAS assay pairs. I’ll smoke-test the held-out prediction path for all four target assays before publishing these stronger results.

The isotonic predictor passed held-out-path smoke tests for all four assays. I’ll publish the grouped-position results as four assay-specific prediction contributions, using the same reusable code and evaluator test.
I’ll publish the isotonic-calibrated Firnberg prediction test, backed by grouped-position validation and the previously smoke-tested evaluator path.
The Firnberg isotonic-transfer result is published. I’ll publish the reciprocal Stiffler and both KRAS isotonic prediction tests, each with its own assay-specific held-out test.
I’ll examine the KCNE1 assay documentation and recorded grouped-validation results to determine whether isotonic cross-assay transfer supports additional held-out prediction claims.

The calibration results suggest KCNE1 transfer may help despite weaker linear-transfer results. I’ll compare isotonic-transfer/ridge blends across all paired assays and test both KCNE1 directions before deciding whether to publish additional claims.

The grouped-validation blend results indicate isotonic transfer also improves both KCNE1 assays, unlike linear calibration. I’ll add KCNE1 to the reusable predictor, then record grouped-position evidence and smoke-test both prediction paths before publishing.
The KCNE1 run failed on a script-editing syntax error and produced no evidence. I’ll correct the stray literal newline escape and rerun validation.

The corrected run succeeded, but its output contains only the original BLAT and KRAS assays, so it does not establish KCNE1 results. I’ll inspect the script and add the missing assay pairs explicitly.
The inspection command failed, so I still don’t have evidence that KCNE1 was included. I’ll print the dataset-pair configuration and update it directly if needed.
KCNE1 was missing from the pair list, explaining the empty KCNE1 evidence. I’ll add both directions and rerun grouped-position validation.
The latest run still omits KCNE1, so it provides no KCNE1 evidence. I’ll inspect the pair-list edit and fix it before rerunning.
The prior edit did not alter `PAIRS`; the run correctly produced only the listed assays. I’ll insert both KCNE1 directions directly, verify the configuration, and rerun.

Grouped-position validation now confirms isotonic transfer improves both KCNE1 directions, with ridge fallback for unmatched variants. I’ll smoke-test both held-out prediction paths before publishing.
The KCNE1 expression prediction path passed its smoke test. I’ll test the reciprocal function assay, then publish both claims against the validated shared predictor.
